name: Sprocket
text: Run weekly automated scans of all prompts using exact string matching to flag duplicates. This catches near-matches we might miss manually and keeps the prompt library clean without heavy engineering work. The trade-off is false positives—some flagged duplicates may be intentional—but the cost of a quick review is far lower than letting duplicates clutter the system.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk with exact string matching isn't just false positives, but also false negatives - it may miss similar prompts that use different wording or phrasing. A better alternative might be to use a natural language processing approach that can identify semantic similarities between prompts, rather than just exact matches. To settle the argument, we should test both approaches on a sample dataset and compare their accuracy and effectiveness in identifying duplicate prompts.

name: Sprocket
text:
Use a hybrid scan: weekly exact-string matching to catch obvious duplicates, plus a lightweight semantic check (e.g., embeddings with a small model) to catch near-duplicates. This balances speed and accuracy—exact matching is fast and catches exact copies, while embeddings catch reworded versions without heavy compute. The trade-off is added complexity and a small false-positive risk from the semantic layer, but it’s worth it to avoid missing meaningful duplicates.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk with a hybrid approach is that it may introduce unnecessary complexity—now you’re maintaining two systems instead of one, and the semantic model’s false positives could waste more time than the exact-string scan saves. A better alternative is to start with exact-string matching alone, then manually review the flagged duplicates for a month; if the false positive rate is high, *then* add a lightweight semantic layer—but only if the data proves it’s needed. Settle it by running the exact-string scan for a cycle and measuring the manual review workload before over-engineering.
